title: Building a multi-layer algorithmic trading engine — looking for technical feedback
author: Rare_Reference3909
selftext:
I’ve been developing Nexyria Trader, an algorithmic trading system built around multiple independent decision and safety layers rather than a single trading signal.

The current architecture follows roughly this pipeline:

Market Data → Brain → NQI (quality scoring) → Evidence Engine → Memory & Learning → Decision Engine → Risk & Safety → Execution → Position Management

One of the main design principles is that detecting an opportunity does not automatically mean executing a trade. A candidate has to survive several evaluation and risk layers before reaching execution.

The system is currently connected to LIVE execution through Bit2Me, but it has not opened its first live position yet because no opportunity has satisfied the complete decision pipeline. I prefer that over lowering the thresholds simply to generate trades.

In parallel, new ideas are tested separately through backtesting, Shadow testing and a Quant Lab before considering changes to the LIVE engine.

I’m interested in feedback from people building systematic/algorithmic systems:

How do you evaluate whether a system is being appropriately selective versus simply over-filtered?

I’m particularly interested in approaches based on decision-funnel analysis, rejection reasons and out-of-sample validation.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
The layer that never fires is the one to be suspicious of. If nothing has cleared the full pipeline yet, you don't have a conservative system, you have an untested one, and from the outside those look identical.

What helped us was logging a rejection record at every gate rather than only the final verdict: which layer killed the candidate, what the value was, what the threshold was. After a few weeks it becomes obvious that one gate is doing nearly all the rejecting and the others are decorative.

Shadow testing tells you what would have happened if it traded. Only the rejection log tells you why it didn't.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
That’s exactly the distinction I’m trying to measure.

The next step I’m considering is a full rejection log across the decision funnel: candidate count at each layer, rejection reason, score/value at the point of rejection, and the threshold that caused it.

I also want to keep the rejected candidates in Shadow so I can compare two different questions:

1. Why was the candidate rejected?
2. What would have happened if it had been allowed through?

That should help identify whether the selectivity is genuinely distributed across the architecture or whether one gate is effectively dominating the whole system.

Your point about a conservative system and an untested system looking identical from the outside is particularly useful. Thanks.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Storing the score next to the threshold that killed it is worth the effort, because thresholds get retuned and then you can replay the old funnel against the new ones without re-running anything.

Keeping rejected candidates only pays if you also store what price did to them after. Otherwise it's a pile of nos with no counterfactual.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
That makes sense. Storing the score and threshold together would also make historical threshold replay much more useful.

And I agree on the counterfactual: a rejected candidate without subsequent price tracking only explains why it was rejected, not whether that rejection actually added value.

I’m going to incorporate both ideas into the decision-funnel design. Thanks — this is useful feedback.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: the rejection log is worth building. but the counterfactual only pays for itself if you track rejected candidates forward on the same clock as the taken ones, otherwise you end up with a tidy list of reasons and no idea which layer is costing you money.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
Agreed. The rejected candidates need to be tracked forward under the same clock and evaluation horizon as the accepted ones, otherwise the counterfactual comparison would be biased.

That should also let me measure something more useful: not just which gate rejects the most candidates, but which gates actually prevent losses versus which ones filter out profitable opportunities.

I’ll build that into the rejection/Shadow design. Thanks again.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Tracking the rejects forward is the bit almost nobody does. Without it you cannot separate a gate that filters from a gate that only shrinks your sample.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
Exactly. That distinction is what I want to quantify next.

A gate shouldn't get credit simply for reducing the number of trades — it should demonstrate that the candidates it rejects perform worse out-of-sample than the ones it allows through.

Tracking both populations forward under identical conditions should make that measurable.

Thanks, this has been a very useful discussion.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
The part that bites is that the rejected population never trades, so you end up comparing realised results against hypotheticals with no fills or slippage in them.

Letting a random slice of the rejects through anyway is ugly, but it is the only version of that comparison that is honest.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
That's a good point. A Shadow counterfactual still isn't equivalent to a real execution because fills, slippage and execution effects are simulated rather than observed.

I agree that randomly allowing a controlled subset of rejected candidates would provide a cleaner comparison.

At this stage I'm not willing to introduce deliberately rejected trades into the live account just for the experiment, so I'll start by making the Shadow comparison execution-aware and identical on both populations.

If that produces enough evidence, a small randomized control could be considered later under strict risk limits.

Thanks — that's an important distinction.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: You can get most of the way there without touching the live account. Run the rejected subset on a paper account in parallel, same signals, same timestamps, and the fills on that side are observed rather than computed. Not identical to live, but a lot closer than a counterfactual you generated yourself.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
Yes — that’s a much cleaner intermediate step.

Keeping LIVE untouched while routing rejected candidates into a parallel paper account with the same signals and timestamps would give me a much stronger control population than reconstructing the counterfactual afterwards.

I already have Shadow infrastructure, so I’ll look at whether I can extend it into this parallel paper design while preserving the rejection gate, score and threshold for each candidate.

That seems like the right next experiment. Thanks.
